sections.h2: Do squatters have rights in Delaware?
sections.html:
In Delaware, someone with no permission can claim title to land only through adverse possession, and the possession has to last twenty years. A short stay in a vacant house creates no ownership, and an owner who acts early has strong options.

The words "squatter" and "adverse possession" never appear in the real actions chapter of the Delaware Code. It works through time limits instead. Title 10, chapter 79 bars a person from entering land unless within 20 years after the person's right or title first accrued, and bars a suit on prior possession unless there was actual possession within 20 years before the action. Delaware courts built the adverse possession elements on that twenty-year rule.

Two very different situations get lumped under "squatters," and the law treats them differently:

  • Long-term occupants with a claim to own: neighbors who have used a strip or a whole parcel for decades, or co-owners and heirs who stayed on in an inherited house.
  • Short-term unauthorized occupants: people who moved into a vacant home or stayed after a lease or permission ended.

The claimant has to prove, by a preponderance of the evidence, possession that is open and notorious, hostile and adverse, exclusive, and actual, and continuous for twenty years. A Master in Chancery laid out that test in the 2020 report in Estate of Waples v. Burton.

  • Open and notorious: public enough that the owner and others are on notice. Furtive possession isn't adverse.
  • Hostile: use inconsistent with the owner's rights. The claimant needn't announce an intent to own, but must act as the owner, shutting others out.
  • Exclusive and actual: absolute exclusivity isn't required, and fences and signs aren't needed in every case.
  • Continuous for twenty years: a bright-line period, though successive possessors can add their time together (tacking) if they are in privity.

Once the claimant meets that burden, the record owner has to show by a preponderance that the use was permissive. The Delaware Supreme Court's 2004 order in Dorman v. Mitchell restated the test as possession in an "open, notorious, hostile and exclusive manner for a twenty-year period" and held that the claimant's title vested in 1991, years before the new owners learned of the property.

Permission defeats the claim. Where a landlord-tenant relationship exists, the use is permissive. In Waples, about 37 years without a rent payment was held to end a tenancy, so the facts on the ground, not labels, decide these cases.

sections.h2: Heirs and co-owners of an inherited house
sections.html:
A co-owner has a harder road. When one co-tenant claims the whole property, the claimant has to show ouster of the others, with more proof than would be needed against a stranger.

Ouster takes three things: intent, adverse possession in fact, and the other co-tenants' knowledge or notice of the adverse claim. In Waples, paying taxes and sewer charges, which began as a voluntary contribution, did not by itself show ouster. The claimant never clearly told the other co-tenants she was excluding them or claiming sole ownership, and their own use of the property was substantial. The report recommended summary judgment for the co-tenants.

For families the lesson is practical. One heir who lives in and pays for an inherited house doesn't automatically become the owner after twenty years. When heirs disagree about who owns a house, a sale can settle it. Talk to a Delaware attorney about who has authority to sell.

It applies sometimes. Under 10 Del. C. section 7903, a person who is an infant, mentally ill or imprisoned when the right accrues may enter or sue within 10 years after the disability ends, even if the 20-year period has run. Section 7904 gives successors in title the same benefit if the person dies while under the disability.

This matters at the edges. If title was held by a minor heir, the clock may not have run against that heir. A title company will want to know about facts like that before insuring a sale.

sections.h2: Removing an occupant who has no right to be there
sections.html:
Use the courts, not self-help. Delaware's summary possession statute, 25 Del. C. chapter 57, lets a landlord or owner file a complaint in the Justice of the Peace Court for the county where the property sits. Section 5703 allows the landlord, the owner or a wrongfully excluded tenant to file.

Grounds include holdover after a lease ends, unpaid rent and lease violations. The court serves the complaint with a hearing notice, and service must happen 5 to 30 days before the hearing. When personal service fails, the court's rules provide for service by posting and mailing.

After judgment, a writ of possession issues once the appeal period passes, with at least 24 hours' notice, and execution happens between sunrise and sunset. A party can seek a new trial or review within 5 days under section 5717. Cases may be sent to mediation under the eviction diversion program in section 5702A.

The Justice of the Peace Court's instructions for a summary possession complaint call for the rental unit address, a short statement of facts, the relief sought and the filing fee. They are written for tenancies. An owner whose occupant never had a lease should talk with a Delaware attorney about the right filing.

If the person is a tenant, a lockout can cost the owner treble damages. Under 25 Del. C. section 5313, a tenant removed or shut out by the landlord or the landlord's agent can recover possession or end the rental agreement, and can collect three times the rent per diem for the period of exclusion, or treble damages, whichever is greater, plus court costs. The statute doesn't apply when the removal happens under a valid court order.

The occupant's status is the deciding fact. Someone who was a tenant, even briefly, may have tenant protections. The lease, rent receipts and messages help a court see what happened.

Criminal trespass is also in the Delaware Code. Third degree, section 821, covers knowingly entering or remaining unlawfully on real property and is a violation. Second degree, section 822, covers a building or an enclosed property manifestly designed to exclude intruders and is an unclassified misdemeanor.

Regular visits and written records are the best defense against a stranger's claim. Adverse possession needs open and notorious use over twenty years, so an owner who checks the house and reacts promptly undercuts a claim long before the period runs.

  • Inspect vacant or inherited property on a schedule and keep dated notes and photos.
  • Secure doors and windows and post the owner's contact information.
  • Give written permission to any neighbor who uses a strip of the land, since permission defeats the hostile element.
  • Pay taxes and keep records of who is in the house.
  • Go to court quickly if an unauthorized occupant appears.

A vacant house with a possible occupant, back taxes or unclear heirs can be hard to sell on the open market. Cash Home Buyers buys houses as-is in many situations, though a title search will show whether a claim has to be resolved first.

faqs.q: How long does adverse possession take in Delaware?
faqs.a: Twenty years. The possession has to be open and notorious, hostile, exclusive, actual and continuous for the whole period, and the claimant must prove each element by a preponderance of the evidence.

faqs.q: Can paying property taxes give someone title in Delaware?
faqs.a: Not by itself. In Waples, a co-tenant's payment of taxes and sewer charges didn't prove ouster of the other owners. The claimant still had to show every element of adverse possession.
Yes. Use with the owner's permission isn't hostile. Once the claimant meets the burden, the record owner has to show the use was permissive.

faqs.q: Can I change the locks on a person living in my Delaware house?
faqs.a: Not safely without a court order if the person is a tenant. Section 5313 lets a locked-out tenant recover treble damages or three times the per diem rent, whichever is greater. Talk to a Delaware attorney first.

faqs.q: Which Delaware court handles removal of an occupant?
faqs.a: The Justice of the Peace Court for the county where the property sits hears summary possession cases under 25 Del. C. chapter 57. Adverse possession ownership claims have been decided in the Court of Chancery and reviewed by the Delaware Supreme Court.
